title: Houthis Claim Missile Strike on Aramco Facilities in Yanbu
excerpt: The unverified claim targets Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea oil port — the linchpin of Riyadh's crude rerouting around the closed Strait of Hormuz — as Brent climbs to $107.80.
body:
• Yemen's Houthis claimed on Wednesday that they carried out ballistic missile strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu and on the Khamis Mushait Air Base.
  • Saudi Arabia and Aramco have not confirmed, denied, or assessed damage from the claim; a Tuesday market report said the 400,000 b/d YASREF refinery in Yanbu was struck.
  • Yanbu is Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea oil port and the terminus of the 750-mile East-West Pipeline, which Riyadh has used to reroute crude around the effectively closed Strait of Hormuz.
  • Brent crude traded at $107.80 a barrel and WTI at $104.69 on the news, as analysts warn the pipeline outage could affect up to 4% of global oil supply.

Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday they attacked Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, the kingdom's main Red Sea oil port — a direct strike at the energy lifeline Saudi Arabia has relied on since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed during the U.S.-Iran war. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree announced two ballistic missile operations: one on the Aramco facility in Yanbu and a second on the Khamis Mushait Air Base in southwestern Saudi Arabia.

The claim, carried by AzerNews from Saree's televised statement, framed the strikes as retaliation for "more than 450" Saudi airstrikes on Yemen this week, following Saudi-led strikes on Hodeidah and Kamaran Island. Saree said the missiles achieved "direct hits," though he did not specify which Aramco facility in Yanbu was targeted — a refinery, storage, or loading terminal — and the claim is unverified. He also claimed the Houthis downed a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib Governorate, which is likewise unverified.

Why Yanbu matters

Yanbu is Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea oil port and the terminus of the 750-mile East-West Pipeline, with capacity of up to 7 million barrels per day. Riyadh has used the pipeline to reroute crude exports around the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively shut since the U.S.-Iran war began in February 2026. The YASREF refinery — a Saudi Aramco–Sinopec joint venture in Yanbu — processes about 400,000 barrels a day and is a major exporter of diesel to Europe and Asia.

A Tuesday market report from Morningstar/OPIS noted that "reports indicated the 400,000 b/d YASREF refinery in Yanbu… was struck by Houthi forces" a day before the formal claim — but neither Saudi authorities nor Aramco have confirmed damage, consistent with Riyadh's pattern of silence on Houthi claims. The East-West Pipeline itself is currently shut after a separate attack, and Kpler data cited in the press says the outage could cut Yanbu export loadings by 2.5–2.7 million barrels per day.

Escalation, step by step

The Yanbu claim is the latest in a sharp escalation. On Tuesday, Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks on the southern Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha, and Taif wounded 13 civilians, prompting Saudi Arabia to warn of a "firm" response and triggering emergency alerts in six cities, including Yanbu. Earlier in September, an attack on Aramco's Jazan refinery was reported, two Saudi oil tankers were attacked in the Red Sea, and the kingdom answered with more than 50 airstrikes on Yemen. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea and seized Perim Island and Mokha, tightening their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

"We will continue our military operations deep inside Saudi territory, targeting Saudi troop buildups, and maintaining the equation of 'a siege for a siege' and 'an escalation for an escalation' until the aggression ceases and the blockade on our beloved country is lifted."

— Yahya Saree, Houthi military spokesperson

Oil markets on edge

Brent crude for November delivery traded $2.12 higher at $107.80 a barrel and WTI at $104.69 as of Tuesday morning, according to OPIS via Morningstar. Analysts at Capital Economics say the pipeline closure could affect up to 4% of global oil supply, while Rystad analysts warn that Red Sea inventory draws can cover Yanbu exports for only two to six days. Saudi Arabia hopes for a partial pipeline restart within days, but full repair of pumping stations could take six to eight weeks.

What comes next

The Houthis have vowed to continue a maritime embargo under a policy of "blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation," threatening to widen operations in the coming days. Saudi civil defense has sounded repeated emergency alerts in Yanbu in recent days, and the coalition has responded to the latest strikes with airstrikes on Hodeidah port. Whether Aramco's Yanbu facilities sustained real damage — and whether Saudi Arabia's firm response goes beyond airstrikes — will determine how far this escalation runs.

For India, the world's third-largest oil importer, the stakes are immediate: every dollar on Brent feeds directly into India's import bill and retail fuel prices, and any disruption to Red Sea shipping hits the route that carries a large share of India's Gulf crude.
